newsitem.title: USA: U.S. option exchanges discussing data overload. [CORRECTED 01:08 GMT 12/9]
newsitem.headline: U.S. option exchanges discussing data overload. [CORRECTED 01:08 GMT 12/9]

text.p: U.S. equity option exchanges are trying to solve bottlenecking problems hampering the dissemination of real-time price data to the public, a senior American Stock Exchange (AMEX) official said.
The options market produces a huge amount of data, inundating information vendors who supply trading room screens, said Joseph Stefanelli, AMEX executive vice president of derivatives.
"That's a problem because vendors are the ones that are disseminating quotes to the public and we want those quotes to get to the public," Stefanelli told Reuters in an interview.

He noted that the option exchanges themselves did not have capacity problems and the Option Price Reporting Authority (OPRA), which compiles data from the exchanges, would soon upgrade its system, probably by October.
"Vendors, though, are still going to be in a position of not being able to accept all this traffic that's coming in," he said.

He added that vendors had said that price information from equity options exchanges alone could sometimes fill up half of their data capacity. AMEX had 50 percent excess capacity on normal days and had not had any problems on peak days.

The problem stems from the fact that each of the 1,500 to 1,600 stocks whose options are listed has at least three strike prices and four expiration months for both puts and calls. Busier, volatile issues have more strike prices.
To make things more complicated, many of the more active options are listed on more than two exchanges.
When the underlying stock price swings, all those option premiums move almost simultaneously.
The measures that the exchanges were looking at included delisting or not quoting inactive issues, Stefanelli said.

Exchanges might, in the future, discuss criteria for multiply listed issues, Stefanelli said. (Corrects to make clear that exchanges would discuss criteria for multiple listings, not try to avoid them) But he noted that this could have anti-competition implications and had to be worked out with the Securities Exchange Commission.
"Anything we do, though, has to be industry-wide," Stefanelli said. "If it were just one of us that did something to curtail quotes, it would not have any impact."
The five exchanges in the talks are AMEX, Chicago Board Options Exchange, Pacific Stock Exchange, Philadelphia Stock Exchange and New York Stock Exchange.
